title: IIT Gandhinagar Uses Machine Learning to Find Materials That Could Convert CO₂ Into Industrial Fuel
excerpt: Researchers screened 56 five-metal combinations using AI-accelerated simulations and identified three ultrathin catalysts that show promise for converting carbon dioxide into carbon monoxide without external electrical input.
body:
• IIT Gandhinagar researchers used machine-learning-accelerated screening to identify three high-entropy MBene materials that could convert CO₂ into carbon monoxide at zero applied electrical potential
  • The computational study, published in npj Computational Materials, narrowed 56 five-metal combinations to three standout catalysts using density functional theory and a MACE ML interatomic potential
  • The approach demonstrates how AI-assisted materials discovery can dramatically accelerate the search for carbon capture and conversion technologies
  • Experimental synthesis and electrochemical testing are needed to validate the computational predictions before any industrial application

A team of researchers at the Indian Institute of Technology Gandhinagar has used machine learning and computational simulations to identify three new materials that could convert captured carbon dioxide into carbon monoxide — a key building block for fuels and industrial chemicals — without requiring an external electrical push.

The study, published in the journal npj Computational Materials, combines two emerging frontiers in materials science: MBenes, which are atomically thin two-dimensional transition-metal borides, and high-entropy materials, which deliberately bring multiple principal elements together to create chemically diverse surfaces.

Screening 56 Candidates Down to Three

The research team considered all 56 equiatomic five-metal combinations drawn from a pool of eight elements: titanium, vanadium, chromium, molybdenum, niobium, tantalum, zirconium, and hafnium. They ran each combination through a multi-stage computational funnel that combined density functional theory (DFT) calculations, formation-energy screening, electronic-structure analysis, and free-energy profiling.

A MACE machine-learning interatomic potential accelerated the process, allowing the researchers to evaluate candidate materials far faster than traditional first-principles calculations alone would permit.

The screening reduced the field from 56 to 18 viable candidates. Three emerged as top performers:

  • CrNbZrMoTiB₅
  • MoZrHfNbCrB₅
  • MoZrHfTaCrB₅

All three showed computationally favorable, downhill free-energy profiles for CO₂-to-CO conversion at zero applied potential — meaning the calculations indicate the conversion could proceed without an additional electrical push under the modeled conditions.

The Cocktail Effect

The researchers attribute the catalytic promise of these materials to what they call the "cocktail effect" in multi-element systems. Rather than relying on a single dominant metal, each atom in the five-metal combination plays a different role in the catalytic process.

The computational analysis indicates that chromium provides a preferred site for CO₂ adsorption, while zirconium and hafnium donate electron density toward the chromium-centered active site. This electronic cooperation helps stabilize the key COOH* intermediate involved in the reaction.

"While previous studies have identified promising MBene catalysts, they generally require an extra electrical boost or generate more complex products such as methane and methanol. Hence, we thought about combining the positives of MBenes with those of high-entropy alloys."

— Sree Harsha Bharadwaj H, PhD scholar, IIT Gandhinagar

The strategy deliberately targets carbon monoxide rather than more complex products like methane or methanol, making the pathway particularly relevant for carbon-utilization systems where captured CO₂ could become feedstock for further chemical conversion.

From Waste Gas to Industrial Building Block

Carbon monoxide is a major chemical-industry building block. It can be combined with hydrogen to produce syngas, a mixture with applications across fuels, chemicals, and energy systems. If CO₂ conversion technologies can be coupled with renewable electricity, they could form part of a broader carbon capture, utilization, and conversion ecosystem — turning what is currently treated as waste into a productive resource.

The researchers used the Param Ananta supercomputing facility at IIT Gandhinagar, supported by India's National Supercomputing Mission, for the computational work.

What Comes Next

The study's lead investigator, Dr. Raghavan Ranganathan, an associate professor in IIT Gandhinagar's Department of Materials Engineering, was clear about the boundaries of the work.

"This possibility is thought-provoking as such approaches may contribute to a future in which captured CO₂ can be circulated back into the economy. While our calculations establish a promising picture, future studies should consider experimental synthesis and electrochemical testing."

— Dr. Raghavan Ranganathan, Associate Professor, IIT Gandhinagar

The research represents a materials-discovery roadmap rather than a finished technology. Catalyst stability, real-world reaction rates, selectivity, synthesis feasibility, and performance under operating conditions all remain to be established through laboratory testing.

The study illustrates the growing convergence of artificial intelligence and materials science in Indian research institutions. Rather than experimentally producing thousands of possible materials and testing them individually, computational tools can identify the most promising candidates first — a capability that could prove essential for tackling a problem as vast as global CO₂ accumulation.
nri_angle: The research at IIT Gandhinagar showcases India's growing role in AI-driven scientific discovery and climate technology, an area of increasing collaboration between Indian institutions and the global research community.
